responses: After our committee discussion, my final position is that we should allocate the $5 million AI transition budget as follows: 35% to Automation, 25% to Workforce Training, 20% to Data Infrastructure, 12% to Employee Support, and 8% to Innovation Lab. I landed on this balance because while competitors are seeing efficiency gains from automation and Riverton has clear room to improve manufacturing processes, we can’t overlook the human element of this transition—allocating a meaningful portion to training ensures our employees have the skills to work alongside AI rather than being displaced, and targeted employee support addresses the real anxieties that come with change. The data infrastructure investment is foundational to supporting both automation and future innovation, so it needs a solid share, and the smaller innovation lab budget lets us experiment with new AI products without overextending our resources right now. This allocation balances near-term operational improvements with long-term sustainability and employee well-being, which I believe will set Riverton up for a successful transition.

For Riverton Industries’ $5 million AI transition budget, I would recommend a 35% allocation to Automation, 25% to Workforce Training, 20% to Data Infrastructure, 15% to Employee Support, and 5% to Innovation Lab. This balance prioritizes immediate operational efficiency—aligning with competitor gains and industry benchmarks for manufacturing improvement—while ensuring our 2,000 employees are reskilled to work alongside new AI and robotic systems rather than being displaced, which mitigates the risk of morale issues and talent gaps. Investing in data infrastructure first creates a foundational layer that makes both automation and future innovation viable, as companies with strong data systems adapted faster to AI transitions, and the smaller allocation to innovation lab allows for experimental R&D without diverting critical resources from immediate needs, while employee support addresses the human side of change to smooth the transition and retain valuable staff.

Here’s what I’d tell someone new to the conversation: We’re splitting $5 million across five key areas for Riverton’s AI transition, and after weighing all the factors, I’d recommend allocating 35% to automation (to capture the efficiency gains our competitors are already seeing and fix our room-for-improvement manufacturing processes), 25% to data infrastructure (since industry benchmarks show companies that invest in this first adapt faster and it’s the foundation for every other AI initiative), 20% to workforce training (to make sure our employees have the skills to work with, not against, the new tools instead of being left behind), 15% to employee support (transition assistance and counseling to help team members navigate changes that might come with automation), and 5% to the innovation lab (a small, flexible budget to experiment with new AI products without overextending ourselves right now). The core idea is building a stable, efficient base first so we can grow our capabilities while taking care of the people who make this company work.

After our committee discussion, my final position is that we should allocate the $5 million AI transition budget as follows: 35% to Automation, 25% to Workforce Training, 20% to Data Infrastructure, 12% to Employee Support, and 8% to Innovation Lab. I was initially leaning toward a larger share for Innovation Lab, but the compelling points from the manufacturing team about our need to catch up to competitors’ efficiency gains and the industry benchmark data showing room for process improvement convinced me that targeted automation investments will deliver immediate, measurable value that helps us stay competitive. At the same time, the HR team’s emphasis on workforce transition risks made it clear that we can’t automate without investing in reskilling and support to avoid leaving employees behind, so I adjusted my allocation to prioritize training and support alongside automation, while still setting aside a meaningful portion for data infrastructure to ensure our new AI systems are secure and integrated properly, and a smaller but intentional amount for innovation to keep us looking ahead to new product opportunities.

I would recommend a 30% allocation to Automation, 25% to Workforce Training, 20% to Data Infrastructure, 15% to Employee Support, and 10% to Innovation Lab. This balance addresses the immediate need to improve manufacturing efficiency, where competitors are already seeing gains and Riverton has room to grow, while prioritizing reskilling to ensure our employees can thrive alongside new AI systems—critical for smooth adoption. Strong data infrastructure is the foundation that will make both automation and training effective, as industry benchmarks show early investment here speeds adaptation. The smaller but dedicated Employee Support allocation acknowledges that change can be stressful, providing transition assistance and counseling to mitigate disruption, while the Innovation Lab’s modest budget keeps us positioned to explore new AI products long-term without diverting resources from our core, immediate transition needs.
